title: A Dual-Uplink Dual-Satellite Architecture for Entanglement Distribution
authors: Charilaos C. Angelidis, Ioannis K. Marmorkos
abstract: Satellite-based quantum links are a promising enabler of long-distance entanglement distribution, overcoming the exponential losses of optical fibers. In uplink architectures, entangled photons are generated at ground stations and transmitted to orbiting satellites, reducing space-segment complexity but introducing significant atmospheric and geometric losses. Single-satellite dual-uplink configurations are additionally limited by the requirement of simultaneous visibility between both ground stations and the satellite.   In this work, we investigate a dual-uplink dual-satellite network architecture and compare its performance with the single-satellite scheme under identical physical assumptions. The proposed topology introduces an inter-satellite link (ISL) that decouples the ground-station separation from the atmospheric uplink geometry. A realistic channel model is employed, incorporating geometric attenuation, atmospheric turbulence, background noise, and Bell-state measurement efficiency. The overall success probability and practical fidelity are evaluated as functions of satellite altitude and ground-station separation.   Our results show that while the single-satellite configuration is suitable for regional-scale networks, it becomes infeasible for large separations due to geometric constraints. The proposed dual-satellite architecture mitigates this limitation and significantly extends the achievable communication distance, representing a key step toward scalable quantum internet infrastructures.
summary: This paper proposes and analyzes a dual-uplink dual-satellite architecture to enable long-distance quantum entanglement distribution. By introducing an inter-satellite link, the design overcomes the geometric limitations that restrict single-satellite systems to regional scales. The results demonstrate that this dual-node approach significantly extends the achievable communication distance while maintaining high fidelity, marking a key step toward a scalable quantum internet.
main_problem: The primary challenge is achieving long-distance quantum entanglement distribution by overcoming the exponential signal losses inherent in terrestrial optical fibers.
main_result: The proposed dual-satellite architecture successfully mitigates geometric constraints, enabling quantum links over intercontinental distances that are infeasible for single-satellite systems.
method: The authors developed a comprehensive simulation framework using a realistic channel model that incorporates geometric attenuation, atmospheric turbulence, background noise, and Bell-state measurement efficiency.
model_or_system: The system models quantum entanglement distribution using ground stations connected via two orbiting satellites and an Inter-Satellite Link (ISL). The architecture compares a single-satellite setup against a dual-satellite setup, which utilizes the ISL to decouple ground separation from uplink geometry.
key_observables: Overall success probability, practical fidelity (F), and the achievable communication distance ($D_G$).
important_parameters: Satellite altitude ($h$), ground-station separation ($D_G$), wavelength ($\lambda$), and atmospheric turbulence parameters ($C_w$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes nighttime operation to avoid overwhelming solar background noise, and the ISL propagation is modeled as a deterministic free-space optical channel in vacuum.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the geometry of the dual-satellite link and compare the success probability and fidelity of the single-satellite versus the dual-satellite architecture as a function of ground station separation distance.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the limitations of single-satellite uplinks. It then introduces and models the dual-uplink dual-satellite architecture, detailing the physical models for uplink and ISL propagation losses. Finally, it compares the performance metrics (success probability and fidelity) of both architectures across varying ground separations.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to quantum optics and quantum networks, providing detailed theoretical modeling of loss mechanisms (atmospheric, geometric, noise) crucial for designing scalable quantum communication infrastructure.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Geometry of the proposed dual-uplink dual-satellite architecture. By utilizing an Inter- Satellite Link (LISL), satellites SA and SB can be positioned at very small zenith angles (ideally θ ≈0) relative to their respective ground stations. This effectively relaxes the geometric constraints of single-node setups, minimizing atmospheric propagation distance such that z ≈h.
Figure 2: Bell state measurement implementation inside the satellite.

Figure 3: Alice sends one qubit to the first satellite. The first satellite passively relays the qubit to the second satellite. Bob sends one qubit to the second satellite. The second satellite will perform the BSM to complete the entanglement swapping protocol.
